clue.text: Sameness I'm not likely to dream about

indicators.note: the dreamy word goes around the clue's own word not, so it signals one piece placed outside another

parts.note: someone moony is dreamy and inclined to drift into reverie
taken as written: the clue says 'I'm not', naming itself the word

explanation.surface: Someone insists that, unlike a dull routine, they are not the daydreaming sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm not' is the clue pointing at its own word, which the dreamy word wraps; 'likely to dream' is a synonym phrase, not a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Monotony is tedious lack of variety, an exact synonym for sameness.

clue.text: Man or no man?

definitions.meaning: the ... of Man, the island in the Irish Sea
John Donne's line 'No man is an island', so no man is one of these

explanation.walkthrough: Both readings name the same thing: Man is one, and Donne says no man is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small island is the kind of land both the Isle of Man and Donne's famous line refer to.

clue.text: Agreement about copper's perspicuity

indicators.note: the word of agreement wraps around the metal's symbol, so it signals one piece placed around another

parts.note: amen is said to express agreement or assent
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A policeman's sharp insight wins general agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the metal, symbol CU.
explanation.definitionFit: Acumen is keen insight, close in sense to perspicuity, clearness of understanding.

clue.text: Quiet girl comes up with "Araucaria's Araucaria"

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the girl's name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Anne is a girl's name
Araucaria is the setter, so his own word for himself is me

explanation.surface: A shy girl turns up bearing the setter's own alias.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Araucaria's' is the setter speaking of himself, giving ME; the second Araucaria is the definition, the name under which John Graham set Guardian puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: Araucaria was the pseudonym John Graham used as a crossword setter, so it is an example of an assumed writing name.

clue.text: Beaten up, which means looking a mess

parts.note: sc. (scilicet) is the abbreviation for 'namely' or 'that is to say'
ragged means tattered and scruffy in appearance

explanation.surface: Someone who has been beaten up is left looking a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: SC, short for Latin scilicet, is used in texts to mean 'that is to say', matching 'which means'.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrag is slang for to manhandle or throttle, so scragged means roughed up or beaten.

clue.text: Mediterranean vessel, a 10 (26)'s subject

definitions.meaning: a vase or jar from ancient Greece, a Mediterranean land
10 is NODE and 26 KEATSIAN: 'a node Keatsian' runs together as 'an ode Keatsian', and one of Keats's odes is on this vessel

explanation.walkthrough: 'A 10 (26)' is a theme device: 'a NODE KEATSIAN' re-spaced is 'an ode Keatsian', an ode by Keats.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote Ode on a Grecian Urn, about an ancient Greek vessel decorated with figures.

clue.text: Fall for a 10 (26)'s subject

definitions.meaning: fall is the American word for the season after summer
10 is NODE and 26 KEATSIAN, so 'a node Keatsian' reads as 'an ode Keatsian', and Keats addressed one ode to this season

explanation.walkthrough: 'For' links the two definitions; 'a 10 (26)' re-spaces as 'an ode Keatsian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's ode To Autumn celebrates the season Americans call fall.

clue.text: Growing girl guerrilla, a 10 (26)

parts.note: Topsy, the girl in Uncle Tom's Cabin, says she just 'growed'
Che Guevara, the Argentine revolutionary guerrilla leader

explanation.surface: A girl who just grew up joins a guerrilla band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A 10 (26)' is 'a NODE KEATSIAN', re-spaced 'an ode Keatsian'; Topsy in Uncle Tom's Cabin famously says she 'just growed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ode to Psyche is one of Keats's great odes, so it is an example of an ode by Keats.

clue.text: Tragic or funny piece for 2

indicators.note: a piece is a part, so the answer is a run of letters taken from inside these words

explanation.surface: A theatre critic asks for a drama, tragic or comic, to fill a slot.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' cross-refers to 2-down, ISLE, so the definition is an island; the letters run across 'tragiC OR FUnny'.
explanation.definitionFit: Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea, so it is an example of an isle.

clue.text: Refusal of Chirac's caused a knotty point

parts.note: no is a refusal
Jacques Chirac was French, and de is French for 'of', the possessive

explanation.surface: A French president's refusal stirred up a thorny issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chirac's' asks for 'of' in French: DE.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a knot or knob, as on a stem, so it is literally a knotty point.

clue.text: Crowd engulfing Lucy and other Tories

indicators.note: the crowd swallows the rearranged letters, so it surrounds another piece

parts.note: a mob is a crowd

indicators.note: the letters are made other than they are, that is, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crowd of Conservatives swamps Lucy and her fellow party members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Other' turns LUCY AND into NDAYCLU, which MOB then surrounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Monday Club is a right-wing pressure group within the Conservative Party, its members being Tories.

clue.text: Historic Earl Sands' lost love

indicators.note: the sands lose something, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the Goodwin Sands are a sandbank off the Kent coast
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: An earl mourns a sweetheart lost on the sands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' looks romantic but is nil, O, which drops out of GOODWIN (the Goodwin Sands, a notorious shoal in the English Channel).
explanation.definitionFit: Godwin was Earl of Wessex and father of King Harold, an eleventh-century nobleman.

clue.text: Water supplies with a distance to travel by post

parts.note: wells supply water
far means a long distance away
go means to travel

explanation.surface: Water is supplied over a long distance by mail.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells Fargo was an American express and mail company of the stagecoach era.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells Fargo ran a mail and express delivery service in the American West, so it stands for the post.

clue.text: Collapse of rig in state of severe pain

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit within the state's name

parts.note: Maine is a US state

indicators.note: a collapse brings the rig down in disorder, so its letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: An oil rig collapses, leaving people in a state of agony.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an oil-rig disaster; the state is the US one in New England.
explanation.definitionFit: A migraine is a severe recurring headache, so it is an example of severe pain.

clue.text: 2 is to hear but not to see

indicators.note: to hear means the word is spoken and we catch how it sounds

parts.note: 2 refers to 2-down, which is ISLE

explanation.surface: A riddle: something you can hear but not see.
explanation.walkthrough: 2-down's answer ISLE, said aloud, sounds like 'I-less', which is heard as 'eye-less': having no eye, unable to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no eyes means being unable to see, as being blind is.

clue.text: Shortage will traumatise the town

parts.note: to scar is to leave lasting trauma
a city is a large town

explanation.surface: A shortage of goods will leave the town traumatised.
explanation.walkthrough: SCAR is read as a verb: what will traumatise someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarcity is a short supply or dearth, a synonym for shortage.

clue.text: Extra publicity for much of meeting

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is publicity

indicators.note: only most of the word is used, so its end is cut away

parts.note: a junction is a meeting point, as of roads

explanation.surface: Publicity fills most of the meeting with extra material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much of' trims ION from JUNCTION, leaving JUNCT.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjunct is something added on as a supplement, so it is an extra.

clue.text: Literarily rounded, more than enough topless in dress

indicators.note: the trimmed word sits inside the garment

parts.note: a coat is an item of dress

indicators.note: losing its top means the first letter is cut

parts.note: ample means more than enough

explanation.surface: A topless figure in a dress is more than enough for anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literarily' points to Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler, where the old spelling survives.
explanation.definitionFit: Compleat is an archaic spelling of complete, used literarily, as in The Compleat Angler, meaning accomplished in every respect.

clue.text: Gun takes a lot of animals in Book 1

indicators.note: the animals go inside the abbreviation for book

parts.note: bk is the abbreviation for book
a zoo is a collection of animals
1 looks like the first letter, A, as in an A1 grade

explanation.surface: A gun is hidden inside a book about lots of animals.
explanation.walkthrough: A and ZOO go 'in' BK; then A for '1', the first, as in A1.
explanation.definitionFit: A bazooka is a portable anti-tank rocket launcher, a type of gun.

clue.text: Tailless rodent's alias is a dish

indicators.note: the rodent loses its tail, its last letter, before the possessive s is added

parts.note: a mouse is a rodent, and the possessive adds an s
aka, 'also known as', introduces an alias

explanation.surface: A mouse without a tail goes by another name: a Greek dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The rodent loses its last letter before the possessive S is attached; 'alias' is the abbreviation for 'also known as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moussaka is a Greek baked dish of minced meat, aubergine and white sauce.

clue.text: Don't start listening to proposals for lots of water

indicators.note: the proposals lose their opening letter
listening means we go by how the word sounds when spoken

parts.note: motions are proposals put to a meeting

explanation.surface: A warning not to start heeding proposals to let in the flood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motions' said aloud is 'mo-shuns'; 'Don't start' drops the opening M sound, leaving 'oh-shuns'. 'Proposals' are motions put to a meeting, not offers of marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Oceans are the vast bodies of salt water covering most of the Earth.

clue.text: The medicine man's medium

indicators.note: the medicine man has, that is contains, the medium in his own letters

explanation.surface: A tribal healer's chosen means of communication.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'man's' as 'man has': the letters run across 'mediCINE MAn'. 'Medium' tempts as a spiritualist, but it is a means of communication.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinema is an artistic and mass-communication medium, the art of the moving picture.

clue.text: Crocod-2?

parts.note: crocodile with its ending replaced by 2-down: a crocodilian reptile that is also an island, the Caribbean group south of Cuba

explanation.walkthrough: Replace '-ile' with 2-down: the answer is both a crocodilian reptile (more usually spelt caiman) and a Caribbean island group.
explanation.definitionFit: A cayman is a tropical American crocodilian, and the Cayman Islands are a British territory in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Brave officer retaining vigour has blessed a 10 (26)'s subject

indicators.note: the officer's letters hold the vigour inside them

parts.note: the MC, Military Cross, is awarded to officers for bravery
elan is dash or vigour
holy means blessed

explanation.surface: A brave and spirited officer is blessed by a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A 10 (26)' is 'a NODE KEATSIAN', re-spaced 'an ode Keatsian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote Ode on Melancholy, so a pensive sadness is the subject of one of his odes.

clue.text: A blow for good liquor

parts.note: ale is a malt liquor

explanation.surface: A good drink comes as a blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a punch but is a strong wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gale is a very strong wind, a blow in the weather sense.

clue.text: Heavens become quiet

parts.note: go means become, as in go mad
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: Good heavens, everyone falls silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Become' gives GO in the sense of going quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavens and gosh are both mild exclamations of surprise.

clue.text: Not quite time in the foregoing for a 10 (26)'s subject

definitions.text: in the foregoing for a 10 (26)'s subject

parts.note: nigh means nearly, not quite

explanation.surface: Almost time for a bird from Keats.
explanation.walkthrough: The foregoing clue is GALE: put the answer 'in' it and you get NIGHT-IN-GALE, the bird of Keats's Ode to a Nightingale; 'a 10 (26)' is 'an ode Keatsian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed in the preceding answer, the word gives the bird that Keats addressed in Ode to a Nightingale.

clue.text: Cooked a steak in poetic style

indicators.note: cooked means doctored or falsified, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A recipe instructs a steak to be cooked in a lyrical manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' belongs to the fodder: A STEAK IN has the eight letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Keatsian describes the style of the poet John Keats, rich in sensuous imagery.
